title: Peripheral artery disease: diagnosis, claudication, and limb threat

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the 2024 ACC/AHA peripheral artery disease guideline. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: At or below what ankle-brachial index is peripheral artery disease diagnosed?
questions.why: 0.91 to 0.99 is borderline. Above 1.40 the arteries are too calcified to compress and a toe-brachial index is used instead, typically in diabetes and kidney disease.

questions.q: What is the first-line treatment for claudication?
questions.why: Walking to near-maximal pain three times a week for at least twelve weeks improves distance more than any drug. Home-based structured programmes are the fallback.

questions.q: Which drugs are recommended for every patient with symptomatic peripheral artery disease?
d: A beta blocker for the legs
questions.why: Aspirin or clopidogrel alone. Low-dose rivaroxaban added to aspirin reduces limb and cardiovascular events in selected patients at low bleeding risk.

questions.q: Which drug improves walking distance in claudication but is contraindicated in heart failure?
questions.why: It is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor of the class that raised mortality in heart failure. Pentoxifylline is no longer recommended because it does not work.

questions.q: Which findings define chronic limb-threatening ischaemia?
a: Rest pain lasting more than two weeks
questions.why: These patients need prompt vascular referral for revascularisation, because the alternative is amputation. Claudication alone is a quality-of-life problem, not a limb-threat one.

questions.q: A leg becomes suddenly painful, pale, pulseless and cold. What is the time frame for action?
questions.a: Hours; it is a vascular emergency
d: No urgency if the foot is still warm
questions.why: Acute limb ischaemia is usually embolic or thrombotic. Heparin is started at once and the vascular team decides between catheter-directed thrombolysis and surgery.

questions.q: When is revascularisation offered for claudication?
questions.a: When symptoms limit lifestyle despite exercise and medical therapy
d: Never; it is only for limb threat
Only when the ankle-brachial index is under 0.5
questions.why: The choice between endovascular and open surgery depends on the anatomy. The medical therapy continues afterwards regardless.

questions.q: Who should have an ankle-brachial index measured to screen for peripheral artery disease?
a: Adults 50 to 64 with diabetes or a smoking history
Anyone under 50 with diabetes plus another risk factor
d: Patients on a statin for any reason
questions.why: Leg symptoms in these groups, including atypical ones, or non-healing wounds, also trigger the test. Half of patients with disease have no classic claudication.

questions.q: Which single risk factor change has the biggest effect on progression of peripheral artery disease?
questions.why: Smoking is the strongest risk factor for the disease and for amputation. All the others are treated too, with the statin as the drug with the clearest benefit.

questions.q: In a patient with diabetes and peripheral artery disease, which routine element of care prevents amputations?
questions.a: Regular foot inspection and protective footwear
questions.why: Small wounds in an ischaemic, neuropathic foot become limb-threatening quickly. Any ulcer in a patient with peripheral artery disease is assessed for revascularisation.

questions.q: How does claudication differ from spinal stenosis pain?
questions.a: Claudication comes on with a predictable distance and eases with standing still
d: Spinal stenosis is relieved only by walking
questions.why: Neurogenic pain eases with sitting or bending forward and can begin with standing alone. Pulses and the ankle-brachial index settle it.

questions.q: Which added antithrombotic reduced major limb events in symptomatic peripheral artery disease?
questions.a: Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily with aspirin
questions.why: The COMPASS and VOYAGER trials showed fewer limb and cardiovascular events at the cost of more bleeding, so it is for patients at low bleeding risk.
